title: How to Check for Liens on a Property Before Buying (Step-by-Step Guide)
excerpt: Buying a property with hidden liens can cost you thousands of dollars and derail your entire deal. Learn exactly how to check for liens on a property before buying so you never get blindsided at closing.
author: AIWholesail Team
tags: how to check for liens on a property before buying
metaDescription: Learn how to check for liens on a property before buying with this step-by-step guide. Avoid costly surprises and protect your real estate investment.
metaKeywords: how to check for liens on a property before buying, property lien search, title search real estate, IRS tax lien search, mechanic lien property, real estate due diligence, wholesale real estate liens, clear title property

sections.content: Imagine closing on what looks like a perfect investment property, only to discover the seller owed $45,000 in back taxes and contractor bills. Suddenly your profitable flip turns into a financial nightmare. This scenario happens more often than most investors realize, and it is almost always preventable. Knowing how to check for liens on a property before buying is one of the most critical skills any real estate investor, wholesaler, or house flipper can develop. A lien is a legal claim against a property, and in most cases, that debt travels with the property — not with the seller.
What Is a Property Lien and Why Does It Matter?

A lien gives a creditor the legal right to a piece of a property until a debt is paid. When you buy a property, any outstanding liens typically become your responsibility. That means a $20,000 mechanic's lien filed by a contractor who never got paid for a roof job could land on your plate the moment the deed transfers into your name. Understanding which types of liens exist — and how to find them — is the foundation of smart real estate due diligence.
The Most Common Types of Property Liens

items: Mortgage liens: The most common type, placed by a lender when a property is financed. These must be paid off at closing.
Tax liens: Filed by the IRS or local government for unpaid federal, state, or property taxes. These are serious and take priority over most other liens.
Mechanic's liens: Filed by contractors, subcontractors, or suppliers who completed work on the property but were never paid.
Judgment liens: Attached to a property when a court rules against the owner in a civil lawsuit, such as a personal injury case or unpaid debt.
HOA liens: Filed by homeowner associations for unpaid dues or fines. Common in planned communities and condo complexes.
Child support and alimony liens: Can be placed against a property owner who has fallen behind on court-ordered payments.

sections.content: How to Check for Liens on a Property Before Buying: 5 Steps
The good news is that most liens are public record. With the right approach, you can uncover them before you commit to any purchase. Here is a straightforward process you can follow on every deal.
Step 1: Start at the County Recorder or Clerk's Office

The county recorder's office — sometimes called the county clerk or register of deeds depending on your state — is your first stop. Most counties now offer online portals where you can search by owner name, parcel number, or property address. Search the property address and the current owner's full legal name. Look for any recorded documents including deeds of trust, notices of default, tax liens, judgment liens, and mechanic's liens. In active markets like Atlanta, Dallas, and Phoenix, many of these portals are updated daily. Check out available deals and property data in your target market at [aiwholesail.com/markets/atlanta-ga](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/atlanta-ga), [aiwholesail.com/markets/dallas-tx](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/dallas-tx), or [aiwholesail.com/markets/phoenix-az](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/phoenix-az).
Step 2: Search the IRS and State Tax Authority Records

Federal tax liens filed by the IRS are not always recorded at the county level first. The IRS files liens with the county recorder in the county where the taxpayer lives, but it is worth doing an independent search. Visit the IRS website and use their federal tax lien search tool, or call your local IRS office. For state income tax liens, check with your state's department of revenue. A seller who owes $30,000 in back federal taxes and never mentioned it is not uncommon in distressed property situations.
Step 3: Check Court Records for Judgment Liens

Judgment liens stem from civil court cases. Search your county court's online docket using the seller's full legal name. Many states allow creditors to attach a judgment lien to any real property the debtor owns in that county. Some investors are surprised to find a property is tied up in an old lawsuit they knew nothing about. Always search using multiple name variations — maiden names, middle names, and business entity names if the seller is an LLC or corporation.
Step 4: Pull a Preliminary Title Report

For serious deals, hiring a title company to run a preliminary title report is worth every penny. This document compiles all recorded encumbrances, easements, and liens against a property into one organized report. Title companies typically charge between $150 and $400 for a preliminary report depending on your market. If you move forward with the purchase, the cost is usually rolled into the final title insurance policy. Title insurance protects you if a lien is missed during the search — an important safety net for any investor.

Pro Tip: When wholesaling a property, always run at least a basic lien search before signing the contract, not after. If you discover a $25,000 tax lien mid-deal, you lose your negotiating leverage. Finding it upfront lets you factor it into your offer price and use our free [Deal Calculator at aiwholesail.com/tools/wholesale-deal-calculator](https://aiwholesail.com/tools/wholesale-deal-calculator) to make sure the numbers still work with the lien payoff included.
Step 5: Do a Name Search Beyond Just the Property Address

One of the most overlooked steps is searching the owner's name independently from the property address. A judgment lien is attached to the person, not just a specific property. If a seller named Robert James Martinez has a $15,000 judgment against him filed in the same county, it automatically attaches to any real property he owns there — including the house you are about to buy. Run a name search alongside every address search. This takes an extra ten minutes and can save you tens of thousands of dollars.
What to Do When You Find a Lien

Finding a lien does not automatically mean walking away from the deal. In many cases, especially in wholesale or distressed property situations, liens can be negotiated down or paid off at closing from the seller's proceeds. A $40,000 tax lien on a property with $120,000 in equity is still a workable deal if your numbers are right. However, a $90,000 lien on a property with $85,000 in equity is a deal-killer unless the lienholder agrees to a short payoff. Always get lien payoff amounts in writing and factor them into your deal analysis. For a full walkthrough on evaluating whether a deal still makes sense after uncovering debts, read our guide on [How to Analyze Real Estate Deals](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/how-to-analyze-real-estate-deals).

"The biggest mistakes in real estate are made in the buying, not the selling. A thorough lien search is not optional due diligence — it is the price of admission for anyone playing the game seriously." — Common wisdom among veteran real estate investors
Liens and Wholesaling: Special Considerations

Wholesalers face a unique challenge. Because you are typically moving fast, often signing contracts before a full title search is complete, the risk of missing a lien is higher. The best practice is to include a due diligence clause in your purchase agreement that allows you to exit if liens are discovered that exceed a certain threshold. Most experienced wholesalers build in at least a 7 to 14 day inspection period for exactly this reason. If you are new to wholesaling and want to build the right foundation, our [Wholesaling Real Estate for Beginners guide](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/wholesaling-real-estate-for-beginners) walks you through every step of structuring deals that protect you legally and financially.
Quick Lien Search Checklist for Every Deal

items: Search county recorder's office by address and owner name
Run an IRS federal tax lien search on the seller's name
Check state tax authority for income and business tax liens
Search county civil court records for judgment liens
Contact the HOA directly if the property is in a community association
Order a preliminary title report for any deal above $50,000
Verify lien payoff amounts in writing before finalizing your purchase price
Include a due diligence contingency in your purchase contract

sections.content: Pro Tip: Many counties now offer free online search portals. Search '[your county name] property records search' to find yours. Bookmark it — you will use it on every single deal.

Knowing how to check for liens on a property before buying is not complicated, but it does require being systematic and thorough on every deal without exception. The investors who get burned are usually the ones who got comfortable skipping steps after a string of clean closings. One missed $50,000 tax lien can wipe out months of profit. Make lien searches a non-negotiable part of your process, and you will protect yourself from some of the most expensive mistakes in real estate.
